analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run universal health care program covering every American with no deductibles or copays.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it was referred to four House committees and subcommittees in 2007 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 1200 would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, the children's health insurance program, federal employee health coverage, and civilian military health coverage with a single, state-administered "American Health Security" program covering every U.S. citizen and lawful resident. It covered hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, dental, vision, mental health, and long-term care with no deductibles, coinsurance, or copayments for most services, and it banned the sale of private insurance that duplicates those benefits. It would have been paid for with a new payroll tax on employers, a new health care income tax, and higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain comprehensive coverage with no out-of-pocket costs for acute and preventive care, kept from birth or immigration, portable across states, with no medical bills or denied claims. The roughly 47 million uninsured at the time would be covered automatically; people with employer or private plans would trade premiums, deductibles, and network restrictions for a public card.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Every U.S. resident; especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a universal entitlement to health care for every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident alien, with automatic enrollment at birth and a portable health security card.

Covers inpatient and outpatient hospital care, professional services, prescription drugs, dental, vision, hearing aids, mental health and substance abuse treatment, and home and community-based long-term care, with no deductibles, coinsurance, or copayments on acute and preventive benefits.

Eliminates Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and CHAMPUS as separate programs, folding everyone into the single program, and prohibits states from allowing sale of private insurance that duplicates its benefits.
Prohibits balance billing, so providers could not charge enrolled patients beyond the program's payment, and pays hospitals through approved global budgets to control costs.
Finances the program through an American Health Security Trust Fund fed by a new payroll tax on employers, a health care income tax, and increased excise taxes on tobacco products.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay a new payroll tax, households would pay a new health care income tax, smokers would pay higher tobacco taxes, and private health insurers would lose the market for plans duplicating program benefits. Higher earners would pay more in taxes than their previous premiums; hospitals and drug makers would accept government-set payments.

drawbacks.text: The bill abolishes Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, federal employee coverage, and CHAMPUS as of December 31, 2008 and moves everyone into a brand-new system, so a rocky transition would have hit tens of millions of people who were satisfied with their existing coverage.
Long-term care is not free: home and community-based services carry 20% coinsurance and nursing facility services 35% coinsurance, waived only for people near the poverty line.

The financing rests on new payroll and income taxes whose rates and real revenue are set out in the bill's tax titles; taxpayers would bear the full public cost that premiums used to spread across employers and individuals, and the tax burden would be visible in every paycheck.

Banning duplicative private insurance and eliminating utilization review removes consumer choice of private plans and one layer of oversight over care decisions, which critics of single-payer proposals of this era warned could mean government rationing and slower access to care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit was the largest available in health policy: universal, comprehensive coverage with no cost-sharing for ordinary care, ending medical debt and uninsurance. The costs were real and concentrated: a large visible tax increase, the risk of a disruptive transition for people happy with existing plans, cost-sharing on long-term care, and the loss of private plan choice. Whether global budgets and government-set fees could control costs without shortening waits was the central honest objection. It never got far enough for any of this to be tested legislatively.

outcome.mechanism: After its sponsor introduced it in February 2007, the House sent it to four committees, which sent pieces of it to subcommittees, and none of them ever took it up; it sat there until the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott and 10 original cosponsors, all Democrats, introduced the bill on February 27, 2007.
It was referred the same day to four committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, and Armed Services.
In the following weeks it was referred to subcommittees on Health (Energy and Commerce), Health (Ways and Means), and Military Personnel (Armed Services).

Its sponsor delivered introductory remarks on March 28 and April 24, 2007, but no hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded, and no further action appears through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2009.
Support never widened past the Democratic wing: all 17 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing health insurance industry and the employer-based system survived untouched, because the bill never advanced; private insurers kept the market the bill would have eliminated, and the tax funds that would have paid for universal coverage were never collected or spent.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and the status quo

for.name: Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, recruited the original cosponsors, and gave introductory remarks on the House floor in March and April 2007.

for.name: 17 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 17 were Democrats, including original cosponsors Dennis Kucinich, Barbara Lee, and Jan Schakowsky.

against.name: House committee chairs of jurisdiction
against.role: Chairs of Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, and Armed Services
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after it was referred to their committees; the record shows no committee action beyond subcommittee referrals for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, but the sponsorship record was entirely Democratic: 1 sponsor and 17 cosponsors, all Democrats, with no Republican support at any point.

industries.note: The bill bans the sale of any insurance that duplicates program benefits and folds Medicare, Medicaid, and employer-based coverage into a public program, eliminating most of the private health insurance market. Insurers' interest lay in the bill's failure, and the status quo that survived is the system they profit from.

Hospitals would be paid through approved global budgets and barred from balance billing, giving up billing discretion, but they would gain universal coverage that ends uncompensated emergency care for the uninsured.

Prescription drugs would be covered for everyone, expanding the customer base, but the government would set payment amounts for drugs under the bill's payment schedules, ending free-market pricing to a single dominant payer.
Employers would stop paying health insurance premiums but pay a new payroll tax instead; they would also lose a benefit tool, though the bill lets them offer extra benefits on top.
